content: Corojo is a specific variety of tobacco that is predominantly utilized in the production of cigars. It was originally cultivated in the Vuelta Abajo region of Cuba. The Corojo tobacco strain was first developed and grown by Diego Rodriguez on his farm, Santa Ines del Corojo, from which it derives its name. For many years, Corojo was extensively used as a wrapper for Cuban cigars. However, its high susceptibility to various plant diseases, particularly Blue Mold, prompted Cuban genetic engineers to create hybrid strains. These hybrids were designed to be resistant to diseases while maintaining the superior qualities required for cigar wrappers. In modern cigar production, both hybrid and pure strains of Corojo are employed. The majority of pure Corojo leaves are now cultivated in the Jamastran Valley of Honduras. In contrast, hybrid varieties are more widely grown and utilized in the industry. This information is based on the article A Tale of Two Seeds by Mark Bernardo, published in the Spring 2004 issue of Smoke Magazine (vol. 9, issue 2).
